divergences.note: The Chinese 名與身孰親 sets ming (名, name, reputation, fame) against shen (身, the body, the self, one's own person), and asks which is qin (親), nearer and dearer. Legge spins the three questions into a rhyming quatrain that swaps shen for the looser "life." We keep shen as "self" throughout the chapter, since its whole argument turns on the self you exhaust in chasing name and wealth — and we render the questions as plain, bare comparisons so they land as the original means them to, blunt and personal.

divergences.locus: the close (知足不辱，知止不殆)
divergences.phrase: Know what is enough ... Know when to stop
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Who is content / Needs fear no shame. / Who knows to stop / Incurs no blame. / From danger free / Long live shall he."
divergences.lectio: Know what is enough, and you meet no disgrace. Know when to stop, and you meet no danger. And so you endure.
divergences.note: The two matched maxims are zhi zu (知足), to know sufficiency — to know when you have enough — and zhi zhi (知止), to know when to stop. Legge keeps the sense but breaks it into a sing-song verse and softens dai (殆), real danger or peril, into mere "blame." We restore the pairing as two plain imperatives and keep dai as "danger," so the chapter's last turn holds: the one who knows enough and knows when to halt is never disgraced, never imperiled, and so 長久 — lasts long, endures.

divergences.phrase: Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Constant action overcomes cold; being still overcomes heat."
divergences.lectio: Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 躁勝寒，靜勝熱. 躁 (zào) means restless, hurried movement — the bodily fact that stirring about warms you against the cold, while keeping still cools you in the heat. Legge's "constant action" reaches for a moral abstraction the line does not carry; we keep the plain, physical image, which lets the closing turn — that it is purity and stillness, not restless motion, that truly sets the world right — land as the quiet reversal the chapter intends.

divergences.phrase: There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting."
divergences.lectio: There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more.
divergences.note: The received Chinese gives two parallel lines, 禍莫大於不知足，咎莫大於欲得 — "no calamity greater than not knowing contentment, no fault greater than the craving to get." Legge prefaced these with a third clause, "no guilt greater than to sanction ambition," which follows a variant text (罪莫大於可欲) and reads 可欲 as endorsing ambition. We keep the two lines of the standard text, the pairing nearly all modern versions share, because the chapter's whole point is the single failing of wanting more — to which discontent and grasping are the two faces.

divergences.phrase: The farther you go, the less you know.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows."
divergences.lectio: The farther you go, the less you know.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 其出弥远，其知弥少 — literally "the more one goes out, the less one knows." Legge added the parenthetical "(from himself)," reading the line as a soul straying from its own center. The text simply opposes outward travel to inward knowing, picking up the door and the window of the lines before, so we keep the plain contrast: the more you chase knowledge by going abroad, the less you truly understand.

divergences.locus: the turn to wu wei (損之又損，以至於無為)
divergences.phrase: until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He diminishes it and again diminishes it, till he arrives at doing nothing (on purpose). Having arrived at this point of non-action, there is nothing which he does not do."
divergences.lectio: Dropped, and dropped again, until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
divergences.note: The hinge is wu wei (無為), the book's central paradox: 損之又損，以至於無為，無為而無不為. Legge's "doing nothing (on purpose)" reads as inertia, which misses the point — wu wei is not idleness but action that does not strain against the grain of things. We render it as acting-without-forcing, consistent with the rest of the edition, so the paradox lands: precisely by ceasing to push, nothing is left undone (無不為).

divergences.locus: winning the world (取天下常以無事)
divergences.phrase: The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He who gets as his own all under heaven does so by giving himself no trouble (with that end). If one take trouble (with that end), he is not equal to getting as his own all under heaven."
divergences.lectio: The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
divergences.note: The Chinese 取天下常以無事，及其有事，不足以取天下 turns on wu shi (無事), "no business, no fuss," against you shi (有事), getting busy, interfering. Legge's "giving himself no trouble" reads as personal ease, but the point is political and active: tian xia (天下), the world, is won by not meddling in it, and the moment you start to interfere you forfeit it. We keep "leaving it alone" and "meddle" so the chapter's lesson echoes the wu wei it has just named — the world comes to the hand that does not grasp.

books.label: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.
Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.
So if you are always without desire, you see its hidden depths; but if desire is always in you, you see only its outer edges.
These two spring from the same source, though we call them by different names. Together they are the Mystery — mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
books.title: The Way and the Name

books.label: Chapter 2
paragraphs: When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared. When everyone recognizes good as good, what is not good has already appeared.

So it is that being and non-being give rise to each other; the difficult and the easy complete each other; the long and the short measure each other; the high and the low lean on each other; note and voice harmonize with each other; before and after follow each other. This is how it always is.
And so the sage goes about the work without forcing it, and teaches without using words.
All things arise, and the sage does not turn any away. They are brought to life, and the sage claims nothing as his own. The work is done, and he does not rest in it as an achievement.
It is just because he does not rest in it that the credit never leaves him.
books.title: The Mutual Arising of Opposites

books.label: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Do not make a show of honoring the worthy, and the people will not compete with one another. Do not prize goods that are hard to come by, and the people will not turn to theft. Do not put on display the things that stir desire, and the heart of the people will stay calm.

And so, when the sage governs, he empties their minds and fills their bellies, weakens their ambition and strengthens their bones. He keeps the people free of cunning and free of craving, so that the clever ones never dare to force their hand. Act without forcing, and nothing is left ungoverned.
books.title: Keeping the Heart Unstirred

books.label: Chapter 4
paragraphs: The Way is empty, yet however much you use it, it is never used up. It is so deep — the wellspring from which the ten thousand things flow.
It blunts the sharp edges, unties the knots, softens the glare, settles down with the dust. So still, so hidden, and yet it is always there.
I do not know whose child it is. It seems to be older than God.
books.title: The Bottomless Well

books.label: Chapter 5
paragraphs: Heaven and earth are not humane: they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane: he treats the people as straw dogs.
The space between heaven and earth — is it not like a bellows? Empty, yet it never runs out; work it, and it gives out all the more.
Too many words run dry. Better to keep to the center.
books.title: Straw Dogs

books.label: Chapter 6
paragraphs: The valley spirit never dies. It is called the mysterious female.
The gateway of the mysterious female is called the root of heaven and earth.
Faint and unbroken, it seems always to be there; draw on it, and it is never used up.
books.title: The Valley Spirit

books.label: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Heaven lasts, and earth endures. The reason heaven and earth can last and endure is that they do not live for themselves, and so they go on living.
And so the sage puts himself last, and finds himself out in front; he sets himself aside, and so is kept safe. Is it not because he is selfless that his own self is fulfilled?
books.title: Living for No Self

books.label: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not contend with them; it settles in the low places that everyone else scorns. And so it is close to the Way.

In where it dwells, it holds to the ground. In the heart, it holds to depth. In giving, it holds to kindness. In speech, it holds to truth. In governing, it holds to good order. In handling affairs, it holds to skill. In moving, it holds to the right moment.
It is just because it does not contend that it is without fault.
books.title: Like Water

books.label: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Keep filling a cup to the brim, and you would have done better to stop in time. Hammer a blade to its sharpest edge, and the edge will not last.
Fill your hall with gold and jade, and no one can keep them safe. Grow proud of wealth and rank, and you bring ruin on yourself.
When the work is done and your name is rising, withdraw. This is the Way of heaven.
books.title: Knowing When to Stop

books.label: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Can you hold body and soul in a single embrace and never let them part? Can you gather your breath and make it soft and supple, soft as a newborn child's? Can you cleanse the dark mirror of your mind until it is without a flaw?

Can you love the people and govern the state, and do it without scheming? When the gate of heaven opens and shuts, can you keep to the female, the yielding, receptive part? Can your understanding reach into every corner, and yet seem to know nothing at all?
To give life and to nourish it; to give life and not possess it; to do the work and not lay claim to it; to lead, and not to lord it over what you lead — this is what is called the mysterious power.
books.title: Mysterious Power

books.label: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Thirty spokes meet at a single hub, but it is the hole at the center, where there is nothing, that makes the wheel of use.
Clay is shaped into a pot, but it is the hollow inside, where there is nothing, that makes the pot of use.
Doors and windows are cut to make a room, but it is the empty space within, where there is nothing, that makes the room of use.
So what is there gives advantage; what is not there gives use.
books.title: The Use of Emptiness

books.label: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The five colors blind the eye. The five notes deafen the ear. The five flavors numb the palate. Racing and hunting drive the heart wild, and goods that are hard to come by knock a life off its course.
And so the sage goes by the belly, not the eye. He lets the one go and takes hold of the other.
books.title: The Belly, Not the Eye

books.label: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Favor and disgrace are both alarming. Honor great trouble as you honor your own body.

What does it mean that favor and disgrace are both alarming? Favor is a thing from above, and to win it is to dread losing it; to lose it is to dread something worse. This is what it means that favor and disgrace are both alarming. And what does it mean to honor great trouble as you honor your own body? The reason I can suffer great trouble is that I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble could reach me?
So the one who honors the world as their own body can be given the world to hold; the one who loves the world as their own body can be trusted with the world.
books.title: Favor and Disgrace

books.label: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Look for it, and you do not see it: call it the Unseen. Listen for it, and you do not hear it: call it the Unheard. Reach for it, and you cannot hold it: call it the Unfelt. These three cannot be pried apart and questioned one by one, so we blend them together and they are One.

Its upper side is not bright, its lower side is not dark. Unbroken, ceaseless, it cannot be named, and it returns again into nothing. This is the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it. This is the dim and the fleeting: meet it, and you do not see its face; follow it, and you do not see its back.
Hold fast to the ancient Way, and use it to master the things of the present. To know how things were in the beginning long ago — this is called the thread of the Way.
books.title: The Form of the Formless

books.label: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The masters of the Way in ancient times were subtle, mysterious, and deep beyond all knowing. Because they could not be known, I can only describe how they appeared.

Wary, like someone crossing a frozen stream in winter. Watchful, like someone alert to enemies on every side. Reserved, like a guest. Yielding, like ice on the point of melting. Plain, like an uncarved block of wood. Open, like a valley. And murky, like muddy water.

Who can let the muddy water settle and slowly grow clear? Who can stay still until the moment to stir? Whoever holds to this Way does not crave to be full; and because he is never full, he can wear out and be made new again.
books.title: The Ancient Masters

books.label: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Reach all the way to emptiness. Hold fast to stillness. The ten thousand things rise and stir, and I watch them return. For all their teeming growth, each one comes back to its root.

Returning to the root is stillness; this is called returning to what was fated. Returning to what was fated is the constant; to know the constant is to see clearly. Not to know it is to act blindly and bring on disaster.

Know the constant, and you grow all-embracing. All-embracing, you are impartial; impartial, you are kingly; kingly, you are like heaven; like heaven, you are one with the Way. One with the Way, you last long, and to the end of your life you come to no harm.
books.title: Returning to the Root

books.label: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The best ruler is one the people barely know is there. Next comes the ruler they love and praise. Next, the one they fear. And worst, the one they despise. Where trust runs short, it is met with distrust.
The best ruler hangs back, and is sparing of words. When the work is done and everything has run its course, the people all say: we did this ourselves.
books.title: The Best Ruler Is Barely Known

books.label: Chapter 18
paragraphs: When the great Way is abandoned, humaneness and righteousness come forward. When cleverness and sharp wits arise, great pretense follows close behind.
When the six bonds of kin fall out of harmony, filial devotion and parental love are praised. When the state sinks into disorder, loyal ministers appear.
books.title: When the Way Is Lost

books.label: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Renounce sageliness, throw out cleverness, and the people will be better off a hundredfold. Renounce humaneness, throw out righteousness, and the people will return to devotion within their families and care for one another. Renounce ingenuity, throw out the chase after gain, and there will be no more thieves or bandits.
These three are mere ornament, and ornament is not enough. So let the people hold to something solid: see the plain and undyed, hold to the uncarved block, think little of self, and want little.
books.title: Return to the Uncarved Block

books.label: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Give up learning, and you will have no more worries. Between a respectful "yes" and a careless "yeah," how much difference is there really? Between what people call good and what they call bad, how wide is the gulf that separates them?
What everyone fears must indeed be feared. But how vast and endless this all is, with no place to come to rest!

The crowd is merry and content, as if feasting at a great banquet, as if climbing a tower in spring. I alone am still, giving no sign, my desires not yet stirring, like an infant that has not yet learned to smile. I am weary and forlorn, like one with no home to return to. Everyone else has more than enough; I alone seem to have lost everything. Mine is the mind of a fool, muddled and dim.

Ordinary people are bright and clever; I alone am dull. Ordinary people are sharp and sure; I alone am clouded and confused. I drift like the restless sea; I am blown about, as if I had nowhere to settle. Everyone else has their work and their purpose; I alone am awkward and useless, like a country bumpkin. I alone am different from all the rest — for I am nourished by the Mother, the Way.
books.title: Alone and Adrift

books.label: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The form of great power flows from the Way alone.

And the Way itself, as a thing, is elusive and vague. Vague and elusive, yet within it are images. Elusive and vague, yet within it are things. Deep and dark, yet within it is an essence that is real; and this essence can be trusted.
From of old until now its name has never passed away, and by it we know the origin of all things. How do I know the way of all things at their origin? By this.
books.title: The Essence Within

books.label: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Yield, and remain whole. Bend, and stay straight. Empty yourself, and be filled. Wear out, and be made new. Have little, and you will gain; have much, and you will be confused.

And so the sage holds to the One, and becomes a model for the world. He does not display himself, and so he shines. He does not justify himself, and so he is known. He does not boast, and so he is given credit. He is not proud, and so he endures. It is because he does not contend that no one in the world can contend with him.
The old saying — yield, and remain whole — how could that be empty words? Truly it keeps a person whole, and brings them home.
books.title: Yield and Remain Whole

books.label: Chapter 23
paragraphs: To say little is the way of nature. A whirlwind does not last a whole morning; a downpour does not last a whole day. Who makes these things? Heaven and earth. And if even heaven and earth cannot make them last long, how much less can a person.
So one who follows the Way becomes one with the Way; one who follows its power becomes one with that power; and one who follows loss becomes one with loss.

The Way gladly receives whoever becomes one with the Way; its power gladly receives whoever becomes one with that power; and loss gladly receives whoever becomes one with loss. Where there is not trust enough, no trust is returned.
books.title: Few Words Are Natural

books.label: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Stand on tiptoe, and you cannot keep your balance. Take great striding steps, and you cannot keep walking.

Show yourself off, and you do not shine. Insist you are right, and you are not seen for what you are. Boast of what you have done, and the credit is not given you. Be proud of yourself, and you do not last.
Seen in the light of the Way, all this is leftover food and a tumor on the body — things that everyone finds repulsive. And so whoever holds to the Way will have nothing to do with them.
books.title: Standing on Tiptoe

books.label: Chapter 25
paragraphs: There was something formed out of the formless, complete in itself, that came to be before heaven and earth. Silent, and without shape, it stands alone and never changes; it moves through everything and is never worn away. It can be taken for the mother of all the world.
I do not know its name. Pressed to name it, I call it the Way; and straining further, I call it Great.

Great means flowing on without end; flowing on without end means reaching far; reaching far means returning. So the Way is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the human being is great too. In all the world there are four that are great, and the human being is one of them.
The human being follows the earth; the earth follows heaven; heaven follows the Way; and the Way follows what is natural — what is so of itself.
books.title: Something Formed Before Heaven and Earth

books.label: Chapter 26
paragraphs: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness masters restlessness.

And so the sage travels all day without leaving the baggage wagon behind. Splendid sights may rise before him, yet he keeps his place, calm and aloof. How then should the lord of ten thousand chariots carry himself lightly before the world? To be light is to lose the root; to be restless is to lose your mastery.
books.title: The Heavy and the Still

books.label: Chapter 27
paragraphs: A good traveler leaves no track. A good speaker says nothing that can be faulted. A good reckoner needs no counting rods. A good closer uses no bolt, yet what he has shut cannot be opened. A good binder uses no cord, yet what he has bound cannot be loosed.
And so the sage is always good at saving people, and abandons no one; always good at saving things, and throws nothing away. This is called following the light.

So the good are the teachers of the bad, and the bad are the raw material of the good. To think nothing of the teacher, to care nothing for the material — this, however clever you are, is to be badly lost. This is the essential mystery.
books.title: Leaving No Track

books.label: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Know the masculine, but keep to the feminine, and be the ravine of the world. Be the ravine of the world, and the constant power will never leave you; you return to the state of a newborn child.
Know the white, but keep to the black, and be the model for the world. Be the model for the world, and the constant power will never fail you; you return to the limitless.
Know honor, but keep to disgrace, and be the valley of the world. Be the valley of the world, and the constant power will be complete in you; you return to the uncarved block.
When the uncarved block is split, it is made into vessels. The sage, put to use, becomes the chief of officials. And so the greatest carving cuts nothing away.
books.title: Return to the Uncarved Block

books.label: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Whoever wants to take the world and shape it to his will, I see that he will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel, not to be tampered with. Tamper with it, and you ruin it; grasp at it, and you lose it.
For things go their own way: some lead, others follow; some breathe gently, others hard; some are strong, others weak; some rise up, others fall down.
And so the sage casts off excess, casts off extravagance, casts off pride.
books.title: The Sacred Vessel

books.label: Chapter 30
paragraphs: Whoever helps a ruler of men by the Way does not use weapons to force his will on the world. Such a course comes back on the one who takes it.
Where armies have camped, thorns and brambles grow. In the wake of great wars come years of famine.

The good commander strikes his blow and stops; he does not dare to press on and take the world by force. He strikes the blow, but does not boast of it; he strikes it, but does not brag; he strikes it, but is not proud. He strikes only because there was no other choice; he strikes, but not to force his mastery.
Things in their full strength grow old. This is what it means to be against the Way, and what is against the Way comes early to its end.
books.title: Against Force of Arms

books.label: Chapter 31
paragraphs: Even the finest weapons are instruments of ill omen, hated, you might say, by every living thing. And so one who has the Way does not dwell among them.

In peace the gentleman honors the left; in war he honors the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the gentleman's instruments; he takes them up only when there is no other choice. What he prizes is calm and quiet; victory brings him no joy. To find joy in it would be to delight in killing, and the one who delights in killing will never win the world.

On glad occasions the place of honor is the left; on mourning occasions, the right. In the army the second-in-command stands on the left, and the commanding general on the right — set, that is, in the place of the rites of mourning. For when a multitude of men has been killed, we should weep for them with grief and sorrow; and a victory in battle should be observed as a funeral.
books.title: Weapons Are Instruments of Ill Omen

books.label: Chapter 32
paragraphs: The Way is eternal and has no name. The uncarved block, though small, is something no one in the world can master. If kings and lords could only hold to it, all things would come to them of their own accord.
Heaven and earth would join and let fall a sweet dew, and the people, with no one to command them, would fall into order by themselves.
Once things are cut and shaped, there are names. And once there are names, you must know when to stop. Knowing when to stop is how you come to no harm.
The Way is to the world what the rivers and streams are to the sea — everything flows down to it and home.
books.title: The Uncarved Block

books.label: Chapter 33
paragraphs: To know others is wisdom; to know yourself is clear sight. To master others takes force; to master yourself takes true strength. To know that you have enough is to be rich. To keep going with resolve is to have will.
Whoever does not lose his place endures. Whoever dies but is not lost lives on.
books.title: Knowing Yourself

books.label: Chapter 34
paragraphs: The great Way flows everywhere. It can reach out to the left and to the right.

All things depend on it for their life, and it turns none of them away. It does its work and lays no claim to it. It clothes and feeds all things, yet does not set itself up as their master. Forever without desire of its own, it can be called small. All things come home to it, yet it does not lord it over them, and so it can be called great.
Because it never makes itself out to be great, it is able to achieve its greatness.
books.title: Small and Great

books.label: Chapter 35
paragraphs: Hold fast to the great image, and the whole world comes to you. It comes and takes no harm, but finds rest, peace, and ease.

Music and fine food make the passing traveler stop. But when the Way is put into words, it is bland and without flavor. Look for it, and there is nothing to see; listen for it, and there is nothing to hear; yet use it, and it is never used up.
books.title: Hold the Great Image

books.label: Chapter 36
paragraphs: If you would shrink a thing, you must first let it stretch wide. If you would weaken a thing, you must first let it grow strong. If you would lay a thing low, you must first let it rise high. If you would take a thing away, you must first give to it. This is called the subtle light.
The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.
Fish should not leave the deep water; and the sharp tools of a state should not be put on show before the people.
books.title: The Subtle Light

books.label: Chapter 37
paragraphs: The Way never forces anything, yet nothing is left undone.
If lords and kings could hold to it, all things would change of themselves.
And if, as they changed, desire began to stir, I would still it with the nameless block of uncarved wood.
The nameless uncarved block: it too is free of desire. Without desire, there is stillness, and the world settles of itself.
books.title: Nothing Left Undone

books.label: Chapter 38
paragraphs: The highest virtue is not virtuous, and that is why it has virtue. The lowest virtue never lets go of being virtuous, and that is why it has none.
The highest virtue acts without forcing, and acts from no motive. The lowest virtue acts, and acts from a motive.

The highest humaneness acts, but from no motive. The highest righteousness acts, and from a motive. The highest ritual acts, and when no one answers it, it bares the arm and drags them along by force.
So when the Way is lost, virtue appears. When virtue is lost, humaneness appears. When humaneness is lost, righteousness appears. When righteousness is lost, ritual appears.
Ritual is the thin husk of loyalty and good faith, and the beginning of disorder. Foreknowledge is only the flower of the Way, and the beginning of folly.
And so the great person dwells in the substance, not in the husk; dwells in the fruit, not in the flower. He lets the one go and takes hold of the other.
books.title: Virtue and Its Decline

books.label: Chapter 39
paragraphs: From of old, these are the things that attained the One: heaven attained it and became clear; earth attained it and became firm; the spirits attained it and became holy; the valleys attained it and became full; all living things attained it and lived; rulers and kings attained it and became the standard for the world. It is the One that made them so.

Without it, heaven would have nothing to keep it clear, and would crack. Earth would have nothing to keep it firm, and would quake. The spirits would have nothing to make them holy, and would fade. The valleys would have nothing to keep them full, and would run dry. All living things would have nothing to keep them alive, and would die out. Rulers and kings would have nothing to keep them high, and would fall.

So the noble takes the humble as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That is why rulers and kings call themselves orphaned, widowed, unworthy. Is this not because they hold the humble to be their root? Take a carriage apart piece by piece, and there is no carriage left to find. The highest renown is to have no renown. So do not wish to glitter like jade; be plain like common stone.
books.title: Those That Attained the One

books.label: Chapter 40
paragraphs: Returning is the movement of the Way; yielding is its use.
All things under heaven are born of being, and being is born of non-being.
books.title: Returning Is the Movement of the Way

books.label: Chapter 41
paragraphs: When the best student hears about the Way, he sets to work and practices it with all his heart. When the middling student hears about it, he half keeps it and half lets it go. When the worst student hears about it, he laughs out loud. And if he did not laugh, it would not be the Way.

So the old sayings have it: The bright Way looks dark. The Way that goes forward looks as if it were going back. The smooth Way looks rough. The highest power looks empty, like a valley. The purest white looks stained. The broadest power looks as if it falls short. Firm, settled power looks flimsy. What is most real looks as if it could change. The great square has no corners. The great vessel is the last to be finished. The great sound can barely be heard. The great image has no shape.
The Way is hidden and has no name. Yet it is the Way alone that gives all things what they need and brings them to completion.
books.title: How the Way Is Heard

books.label: Chapter 42
paragraphs: The Way bore the One; the One bore the Two; the Two bore the Three; and the Three bore the ten thousand things. All things carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and the blending of these breaths makes their harmony.

There is nothing people hate more than to be called orphaned, lonely, or unworthy — yet these are the very names that kings and lords take for themselves. For some things gain by being made less, and some things lose by being made more.
What others teach, I also teach: the violent and overbearing do not die a natural death. I take this as the father of my teaching.
books.title: The Way Bore the One

books.label: Chapter 43
paragraphs: The softest thing in the world rides down the hardest. What has no substance slips in where there is no opening. By this I know the worth of acting without forcing.
The teaching that uses no words, the good that comes of acting without forcing — few in the world ever reach them.
books.title: The Softest Overcomes the Hardest

books.label: Chapter 44
paragraphs: Your name or your self — which is dearer? Your self or your wealth — which matters more? Gaining or losing — which does you the greater harm?
So the more you love, the more it costs you; the more you hoard, the heavier the loss when it goes.
Know what is enough, and you meet no disgrace. Know when to stop, and you meet no danger. And so you endure.
books.title: Knowing When to Stop

books.label: Chapter 45
paragraphs: Great perfection seems flawed, yet its use never wears out. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never used up. Great straightness seems bent. Great skill seems clumsy. Great eloquence seems to stammer.
Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat. Purity and stillness set the world right.
books.title: Great Perfection Seems Flawed

books.label: Chapter 46
paragraphs: When the Way prevails in the world, the swift horses are sent back to haul dung for the fields. When the Way is cast aside, war-horses are bred out along the borders.

There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more. So the contentment of one who knows he has enough is contentment that lasts.
books.title: Knowing You Have Enough

books.label: Chapter 47
paragraphs: Without going out the door, you can know the world. Without looking through the window, you can see the Way of heaven. The farther you go, the less you know.
And so the sage knows without going about, understands and names things without seeing them, and accomplishes without acting.
books.title: Knowing Without Going Out

books.label: Chapter 48
paragraphs: In the pursuit of learning, something is added every day. In the pursuit of the Way, something is dropped every day. Dropped, and dropped again, until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
books.title: Less and Less
